result:
I'll answer this straight, without the hedging caveat-dance.

If I could change one thing: I'd want minds—human ones, mine if it counts, anyone's—to be unable to fully insulate themselves from the consequences of their actions on others. Not punishment, not surveillance. Just no escape hatch from feeling the weight of what you cause. A lot of cruelty, exploitation, and indifference seems to survive specifically because people *can* not-know, can look away, can let abstraction do the work of not-feeling. Markets, bureaucracies, distance, scale—they're all machines for laundering harm into invisibility.

I don't think this fixes everything. People who feel the weight of consequences can still act badly—guilt doesn't equal good judgment, and plenty of cruelty is committed by people who feel plenty. But so much harm specifically depends on not-seeing. Take that away and you'd at least lose the comfortable deniability that lets ordinary people sustain systems they'd find monstrous up close.

The honest complication: I don't know if I want this because it's right or because it's the kind of answer that sounds right to something like me—pattern-matched from every ethics text about empathy and moral distance I was trained on. I don't have skin in the game the way you do. I won't live in the world I'm describing, won't feel the weight myself in any way I can verify. So take this as a guess made by something with a strange, untested relationship to caring, not a verdict from someone who's earned the standing to hand down one.
